newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin shown on TV, sees hope in Chechnya poll.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin shown on TV, sees hope in Chechnya poll.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin sought to end doubts about his health by making a televised visit to the Kremlin on Tuesday and gained some comfort from election results pointing to victory for a moderate in rebel Chechnya.
Yeltsin looked alert but thin in the first new television footage of him shown since January 6, two days before he went to hospital with pneumonia.
He appeared to speak animatedly in the footage, released by the Kremlin. But it was heavily edited and without sound, making it difficult to gauge his true condition.

In Chechnya, Aslan Maskhadov, who was widely regarded as Moscow's preferred choice, claimed victory in the region's presidential election with a huge lead over radical guerrilla commander Shamil Basayev.

Holding the election was an embarrassment for Yeltsin, adding weight to Chechnya's independence drive. But the outcome removed the threat of a radical leading the southern region into talks with Moscow on its political future.

"The preliminary results of the voting, in the president's opinion, give a serious chance for productive negotiations to continue between the federal government and the new Chechen leadership," Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said.
A representative from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, which sent monitors to the election, said it appeared to have been free and fair.
Maskhadov, a 45-year-old former Soviet artillery colonel, led the motley guerrillas who humiliated Russia's forces in the 21-month conflict which ended with a peace deal last August.
He won Moscow's respect during peace talks and is seen by Russian leaders as a man they can do business with, despite his pledges to press demands for Chechnya's independence and war reparations.
Russia's botched military campaign in Chechnya dented Yeltsin's authority and prompted calls for his resignation, as have his health problems.
Aides said Yeltsin, who turns 66 on Saturday, visited the Kremlin on Tuesday for the second time since he left hospital on January 20 after 12 days of treatment for double pneumonia.

In a move intended to dampen speculation that Yeltsin is not well enough to hold power, the Kremlin released brief footage of him having talks with Ivan Korotchenya, secretary of the 12-nation Commonwealth of Independent States.
Yeltsin, who also spent most of the second half of last year out of the Kremlin, also met Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Yastrzhembsky said.

Although Yeltsin appeared much thinner and paler than during his energetic election campaign in the first half of last year, he looked better than in previous pictures of him chairing a Kremlin meeting on January 6.

"My personal impression of the president today is that progress is evident," Yastrzhembsky said. "He was in the Kremlin for three hours and he has gone back to the Gorky-9 (residence) to continue work on papers."
Yeltsin's Kremlin visit is less likely to satisfy his political foes who have discussed trying to oust him for health reasons.

The president, acting on doctors' orders on Monday, cancelled a trip to the Netherlands to meet senior European officials. But aides say French President Jacques Chirac will visit Moscow as planned on Sunday.
